articles.title_orig: The Supreme Court revives a controversial data system for citizenship checks
articles.title_zh: The Supreme Court revives a controversial data system for citizenship checks
articles.content_orig:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference July 1 in New York. David Delgado/AP hide caption
The U.S. Supreme Court has for now revived a federal data system the Department of Homeland Security revamped into a tool to check the citizenship of millions of Americans on state voter rolls. The tool has mistakenly flagged some eligible voters as potential noncitizens.
The news comes as the Trump administration has been pouring resources into searching for noncitizens on voter rolls ahead of the upcoming election.
Many states uploaded their voter lists to the expanded version of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements data system — known as SAVE — sharing that voter information with the federal government. Tens of millions of voter records were run through SAVE before it was blocked by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., in June.
The Supreme Court's decision clears the way for the administration to again use the revamped SAVE in its hunt for noncitizens on voter rolls, as well as in its unprecedented project of compiling lists of adult citizens in each state .
Any impact on the midterm elections is unclear. Federal law bans states from "systematically" removing voters from rolls within 90 days of a federal election.
The Trump administration and Republican state officials have argued that statute should not apply to removing noncitizens who were improperly registered. And the federal government argued to the Supreme Court that at a minimum, the updated SAVE should be able to be used for individual removal decisions ahead of an election.
In siding with the Trump administration, the court's majority wrote that the lower court order that halted the expanded SAVE prevents the federal government "from using the modified SAVE program to conduct individualized inquiries, which are permitted under federal law during this [90-day] period. The District Court's order thus inhibits the Federal Government's efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections."
The Supreme Court's three liberal justices dissented from the ruling, and would have denied the Trump administration's stay application.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson authored the dissent, writing about the "majority's omission of any consideration of the harms that might occur if the modified SAVE system is allowed to continue operating. The District Court highlighted such harms, noting the risk that States might cancel the voter registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens or force such persons to provide proof of citizenship before voting."
The coalition of organizations that challenged the SAVE overhaul last year, which includes the League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center, put out a statement on Friday that said litigation in the case is ongoing.
"Today's decision is profoundly disappointing, as it puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections," the statement reads. "However, this case is not over. The D.C. district court ruled that the expanded SAVE program violated multiple laws. We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans' voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands."
SAVE is a 40-year-old federal data system that was created to check the immigration status of noncitizens to determine their eligibility for public benefits.
Then, DHS overhauled SAVE last year by linking it for the first time with Social Security Administration records, which include most Americans. The overhaul also allowed bulk queries to SAVE, and DHS encouraged states to upload their entire voter rolls to SAVE to verify those registered are U.S. citizens and not listed as deceased in federal records.
In June, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, blocked use of the modified version of SAVE , finding that its aggregation and disclosure of sensitive data violated the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act and the Administrative Procedures Act.
"The federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," she wrote.
After an appeals court panel refused to stay the lower court's decision in a 2-1 vote, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer appealed to the Supreme Court earlier this month .
In his appeal, Sauer wrote that since May 2025, the updated version of SAVE has verified more than 65 million voters across 26 states, and has flagged 28,635 as potential noncitizens.
"The district court's order, however, makes it harder to detect ineligible voters, undermining the integrity of federal elections and public confidence in the results of those elections," he wrote.
The League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center — which are represented in the case by Democracy Forward, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington and the Fair Elections Center — argued in a brief to the Supreme Court that Congress has not authorized the federal government to create a "master database of U.S. Citizens," nor does it have data that could do that accurately. The brief added that multiple statutes restrict repurposing and sharing Americans' sensitive data.
"Disregarding these laws, the government has recklessly created an error-laden master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans' privacy and voting rights," the groups wrote.
They wrote that even though 65 million voters had been verified by the revamped SAVE, the government had not yet released the system's error rate, or how many Americans' citizenship was misrepresented "and who consequently have been forced to reverify their citizenship to retain their voter registration or obtain government benefits."
Even though Election Day is just over a month away and voting is underway, the Trump administration could try to make use of the expanded version of SAVE right away in its quest to check registered voters' citizenship.
An executive order President Trump signed in March calls for federal agencies to consult SAVE data, along with other federal records, to create state-by-state lists of adult U.S. citizens. The same order directs the U.S. attorney general to prioritize investigating and prosecuting election officials who provide ballots to ineligible voters. Even though the executive order says such state lists are to be completed 60 days before an election and that deadline has already passed, federal officials have indicated the project is still underway – although it is facing a legal challenge.
Eligible voters have been erroneously flagged by SAVE, which has been unable to confirm the citizenship of certain categories of foreign-born people who become U.S. citizens.
After Texas ran its entire voter list of 18 million voters through SAVE, the system flagged 2,724 voters as potential noncitizens. County election officials then gave those individuals 30 days to prove their citizenship and, following state law, removed anyone who did not respond in time.
As NPR first reported in December , that effort resulted in citizens being removed from the rolls. Anthony Nel, whose story NPR highlighted in that reporting, gave a declaration in this lawsuit.
A recent press release from the Texas secretary of state revealed that of the 2,724 voters that were initially flagged by SAVE as potential noncitizens, some 20% were later found to be citizens who were reinstated. The same release said the office referred 117 cases identified by SAVE, or 4.2% of those flagged, for investigation for possible noncitizen voting.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi visit to Washington wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi visit to Washington wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.content_orig:
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."
The White House released the invite list for Thursday's state dinner, which includes high-level government officials and several of the world's wealthiest tech executives.
Among the notable people on the guest list are Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet-level officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Mr. Trump's children – Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany – also got invites.
The world's richest person, Elon Musk, is on the list. NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Apple's Tim Cook, Google's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and TikTok investor Jeff Yass also got invites.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also attending. (Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.)
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump walked out of the White House's North Portico shortly after 7 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, then arrived in a car and posed for photos with the Trumps before walking inside.

articles.title_zh: S&P 500 rises, heads for winning week despite Treasury yield surge: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields rose on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Federal Reserve commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up more than 4 basis points to 5.209% after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was higher by more than 5 basis points at 5.516% after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was up less than 1 basis point at 4.897%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors also weighed a global bond sell-off this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a 66% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."
On Friday, durable goods orders in August came in relatively unchanged , while economists polled by Dow Jones had expected a decline of 0.3%. Additionally, consumer sentiment plummeted in September.

articles.title_orig: Ketanji Brown Jackson criticizes supreme court’s handling of emergency docket
articles.title_zh: Ketanji Brown Jackson criticizes supreme court’s handling of emergency docket
articles.content_orig:
The justice called out her colleagues in a speech she made at the UDC school of law, hours after Trump filed his latest request
US supreme court justice Ketanji Brown Jackson acknowledged serious concerns about her colleagues’ handling of emergency requests, the method Donald Trump often uses to seek approval from the court.
Jackson, one of the three liberal members of the supreme court, criticized the justices’ willingness to issue rulings via the “shadow docket”, saying it undermines the public’s faith in the judicial system.
“There is a serious concern that the supreme court’s modern stay practices are having a disruptive and potentially corrosive effect,” Jackson told faculty and students at the University of the District of Columbia’s David A Clarke school of law on Thursday.
Her comments came just hours after the Trump administration filed its latest emergency request – this time asking justices to allow officials to continue deporting immigrants to countries other than their own .
The emergency docket, sometimes also referred to as the “shadow docket”, is where plaintiffs can request immediate relief from the supreme court in consequential cases.
Justices can quickly grant or dismiss requests without conducting the same legal review that is typically required in merit cases or providing a lengthy explanation to the public.
The Trump administration has used the method to rapidly push forward the US president’s agenda. Since returning to office in January 2025, the administration has filed more than 30 emergency requests. Many have been granted.
Via emergency requests, the conservative wing of the supreme court has allowed Trump to temporarily end protections for migrants seeking asylum, eliminate transgender rights, roll back environmental protections, fire the officials in charge of independent federal agencies and more.
The justices have faced criticism for their handling of emergency requests from members of Congress and the public.
However, in July, justice Elena Kagan, another member of the liberal wing of the court, told Congress that she thought they were improving its handling of requests by providing some justification.
Jackson pointed to that on Thursday, telling the audience that while the court “began to explain more”, it was “still not the full kind of explanation” that cases receive on the merits docket. “If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end-run around the standard review process,” she added.
As Jackson critiqued the court’s current methods, which have become more prominent under the second Trump administration, three of her colleagues dined with Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping at the White House.
Chief justice John Roberts and justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett joined other officials for the state dinner to welcome Xi.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo warns of AI threat to humanity at start of three-day France visit
articles.content_orig:
Pontiff says artificial intelligence must remain at service of people in first official papal visit to country in 18 years
Pope Leo has warned against losing humanity in a “paradise of machines” as he addressed global concerns over the dangers of artificial intelligence at the start of a three-day visit to France.
“If we are to avoid losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines invading and conditioning our daily lives, there is an urgent need for people to be educated in ethical discernment, capable of seeing what is morally right,” he said in a speech at the Élysée.
At a second address on Friday, the 71-year-old head of the Catholic church insisted that new technologies must “remain at the service of the human person rather than becoming yet another instrument of domination and injustice” in remarks to a gathering at the Paris headquarters ⁠of the UN culture and education body, ⁠Unesco.
“Every science risks losing its proper meaning when pursued without ethics,” he said. “Certain artificial systems have even been given the name of our human faculty of thought: intelligence. At the same time, however, our ideas and relationships risk being impoverished by a process of dehumanisation.”
He added: “While intelligence is attributed to computational systems, we struggle to recognise the inalienable dignity of human persons whose lives are judged according to the criterion of efficiency and when deemed no longer productive, rejected and discarded.”
Leo also criticised world leaders who disrespect the ⁠rule of ⁠law, without naming individuals. “Instead of ​respecting ‌the law, ‌those in power invoke ‌it when it serves their interests and disregard it when it restrains them, treating even justice itself ‌as though it were a commodity to be ​bought and sold,” he said.
Leo, who became pope in 2025, ⁠has been critical of the direction ​of ​global leadership in ​recent months. He ​said ‌the world was “being ​ravaged ​by a handful of tyrants” last April.
The first official papal visit to France in 18 years comes as Emmanuel Macron’s decade in office draws to an end ahead of next spring’s French presidential election, for which the far-right, anti-immigration Marine Le Pen is polling high. Pope Francis did not make a full state visit to France during his 12-year pontificate and refused to join the inauguration of the rebuilt Notre Dame Cathedral in 2024.
After France passed legislation in June granting some adult patients the right to assisted dying , the pontiff said he was concerned by trends “that risk turning science and technology into profit-driven ventures promoting genetic manipulation, surrogacy, the trade in human organs or the possibility of arranging one’s own death.”
A key moment of the three-day visit will be a giant outdoor mass on Saturday, led by the pontiff at Place de la Concorde.
The pope, whose paternal grandmother was born in France, on Friday urged Paris to remain a “tireless champion of peace” worldwide. On Monday, he will deliver a speech on European peace in the eastern city of Metz as Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues into its fifth year.
Leo called on the world not to ⁠become indifferent to the pain caused by “the scourge of war”.
He told Macron and other French politicians: “I urge you ‘… never to grow resigned to the prospect of war or to ⁠consider it ‘inevitable’.”
Leo will also visit Lourdes, a pilgrimage site for Christians worldwide, where he will privately meet seven victims of clerical sex abuse. After some survivors’ groups suggested a larger number of survivors should have been canvassed, the Catholic church said the pontiff was seeking in-depth dialogue with individuals.
France’s Catholic bishops’ conference has agreed to provide compensation after a 2021 report estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over 70 years by priests or other church-related figures in France. The report described a “systemic” cover-up by church officials.
In recent years, further accusations have emerged, including against workers at the elite Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram , near Lourdes.
On his flight to Paris, Pope Leo told reporters they were welcome to cover him, as he responded to the Trump administration’s attempt to bar US media from the White House and affirmed the importance of journalists covering public figures.
Asked by a CNN reporter about Donald Trump’s attempt to bar CNN and other reporters, Leo said the media were welcome on his plane. “I am very happy that here, you are all welcome,” he said.

articles.title_orig: U.S. appeals court upholds Pentagon designation of Anthropic as supply chain risk
articles.title_zh: U.S. appeals court upholds Pentagon designation of Anthropic as supply chain risk
articles.content_orig:
A federal appeals court panel in Washington, D.C., on Friday upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic , dealing a blow to the artificial intelligence company in its months-long battle with the Trump administration.
The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.
"The Department had ample support for its conclusion that the continued integration of Claude into the Department's information systems, by the Department or its contractors, presented a statutorily covered national-security risk," Judge Gregory Katsas wrote in the majority opinion for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, which Judge Neomi Rao joined. Katsas and Rao were appointed by President Donald Trump .
Judge Karen LeCraft Henderson, who was appointed by former President George H.W. Bush, dissented.
In March, the DOD labeled Anthropic a supply chain risk , meaning the company purportedly threatened U.S. national security, after negotiations about how the military could use its Claude AI models spiraled out of control. The designation prevents the U.S. military from using Anthropic's models and blocks defense contractors from using them in their work with the agency.
Anthropic's relationship with the Trump administration has been fraught ever since, and Trump has repeatedly slammed company's CEO Dario Amodei on social media. Amodei recently drew Trump's ire by calling for an industry wide slowdown , and he was not invited to the glitzy state dinner the White House hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
"The Trump Administration has stopped AI "people" from doing bad, or potentially bad, "things," like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a "perfect little angel" - and we will continue to do so!," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social on Monday.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in U.S. District Court in San Francisco and in the D.C. Circuit Appeals Court in March, seeking to reverse its blacklisting. The DOD relied on two distinct designations to justify its supply chain risk action, which meant they had to be litigated in two separate courts.
A San Francisco federal judge ruled last month that one designation was illegal. The ruling Friday by the D.C. appeals court upheld the second designation.
"We respectfully disagree with the court's decision," an Anthropic spokesperson told CNBC in a statement. "Another federal court has already held the government's parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review."
The appellate panel said it would delay the decision from taking immediate effect to give Anthropic time to petition the same panel for a rehearing or to seek an en banc rehearing of the case, by all of the judges on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. Anthropic could also ask the Supreme Court to take the case.
Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.
The DOD wanted Anthropic to grant the military unfettered access to its models across all lawful purposes, while Anthropic wanted assurance that its technology would not be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance. They were unable to come to an agreement, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of attempting to "to seize veto power over the operational decisions of the United States military."
Katsas said Friday that Hegseth raised the "deeply sobering" idea that "overly constrained" AI models could shut down unexpectedly, as well as the potential that Claude might be "subject to manipulation." While Anthropic refuted those claims, Katsas said decision-making authority ultimately rests with Trump and Hegseth.
"In our Republic, it is the President and the Secretary of War who must determine how best to balance the competing risks," Katsas wrote. "In doing so here, the Secretary did not transgress any limits on his authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution."

articles.title_zh: Ed Sheeran's next US concerts cancelled due to bad weather
articles.content_orig:
The singer was set to perform at Gillette Stadium as part of his Loop tour, which faces backlash over Macklemore’s removal following his pro-Palestinian comments
Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts , have been canceled due to severe weather, adding further complication to a tour embroiled in controversy.
On Friday, Sheeran’s tour promoter, Messina Touring, said : “Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium.”
“The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority,” Messina Touring added.
Sheeran had been scheduled to perform at the 64,628-seat arena on Friday and Saturday as part of his Loop tour.
The cancellations come after weeks of controversy surrounding the tour, after efforts by the stadium’s billionaire owner, Robert Kraft, to rally other stadium owners and pressure Sheeran to remove Macklemore from his tour’s opening acts after the rapper called for a “free Palestine” at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
Macklemore’s comments, including, “‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” drew the ire of pro-Israel organizations, which accused the singer of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda”. The backlash prompted Kraft – the owner of the New England Patriots and a major donor to Israel – to pressure Sheeran to remove Macklemore from the tour.
Macklemore is an avid supporter of Palestinian rights and has frequently condemned Israel’s deadly war across Gaza, which has forcibly displaced 2 million survivors since 2023 while killing at least an estimated 74,000 Palestinians.
Following Macklemore’s removal from Sheeran’s Loop tour, both Sheeran and Kraft faced widespread public backlash. Sheeran subsequently issued a statement saying: “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine. Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.”
Sheeran added that he would “never … abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”
The supporting acts, including four openers and Sheeran’s live band, withdrew from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore shortly afterward.
The Irish band Beoga, which performed as Sheeran’s backing band, said it opposed the “silencing of Macklemore by Zionist lobbies”. Aaron Rowe, an Irish singer who was scheduled to perform on the 10 remaining tour dates in North America, said: “As Irish people, we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children.”
American singer Finneas also voiced support for Macklemore, saying: “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran . I stand with Palestine and its people.”
Danish pop band Lukas Graham also pulled out, saying: “Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge.”
Macklemore subsequently announced that he would donate the $1m salary he earned from Sheeran’s tour to organizations supporting relief efforts across Gaza and invited Kraft to match his donation.
In response, Kraft issued a statement saying that Sheeran had “called me and asked me to commit $2m to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis”, without specifying which groups would receive any donated money.
Macklemore has also since announced his own “Free Palestine” tour, with three dates scheduled next month in Dublin, Paris and London, with “all proceeds benefiting organizations supporting Palestine and the Palestinian movement”.

articles.title_zh: Nor’easter Could Bring Heavy Rain, Winds, and Flooding to East Coast
articles.content_orig:
An early-season nor'easter will bring coastal flooding, high surf, strong winds and rain to parts of the East Coast through the weekend, with impacts from North Carolina to New England.
New York City and especially Boston need to stay weather aware this weekend, and prepare the same as you would for a tropical storm.
The nor'easter is strengthening as it heads north. The map below shows the winds and rain as the low moves north along the East Coast.
Wind gusts over 30 mph, with occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph, are occurring along the coast from southeast New England to the Outer Banks of North Carolina.
( MORE: Nor'easter tracking maps )
Coastal flooding is also occurring at high tide from parts of Long Island to North Carolina.

Here's a general timeline of the storm and its impacts over the next several days.
The map below shows coastal flood alerts have been issued by the National Weather Service. These alerts include Atlantic City, Long Island, the Norfolk metro area, Ocean City (Maryland and New Jersey), downtown Boston, Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.
The most significant coastal flooding will be from the northern Outer Banks of North Carolina to the  Jersey shore, including the Virginia Tidewater, as well as Chesapeake Bay and Delaware Bay.
(WATCH: Nor'easter waves slam stilt homes on the Outer Banks )
This flooding will happen for multiple high tides into the weekend, in these areas. It will also be boosted by Saturday's full moon, with some of the highest astronomical tides of the month.
Given this repeated battering from high surf, beach erosion is expected along stretches of these beaches, potentially reaching extreme levels for some areas.
At least minor coastal high tide flooding will also develop in parts of New England by late Friday into the weekend.
One bit of good fortune with this storm is that its rainfall will be spread out over several days, rather than arriving in one short deluge.
While we expect the most rain to fall from southern New England to New Jersey, those rainfall totals in the map below will be stretched out through Monday.
That means any rainfall flooding should be mainly local in nature in some of the traditional urban trouble spots.
That rainfall could also add to any coastal flooding at high tide through Sunday.
In the New York City metro area, the heaviest rainfall is expected in Long Island, with less rain as you go west into the outer New Jersey suburbs.
High wind warnings are in effect for parts of southeast New England, including Boston and Providence, and also along coasts of Delaware and New Jersey. In these areas, gusts up to 60 mph are possible through Saturday night.
In these areas, some tree damage and power outages are most likely. Ground soaked from the nor'easter's rain, as well as trees still with leaves will only enhance this threat of tree damage and outages.
Otherwise, occasional gusts from 40 to 50 mph are possible from North Carolina's Outer Banks to other parts of coastal New England. Some sporadic power outages and tree limb damage are also possible in these areas.

Some gusts topped 40 mph along the coast from southern Massachusetts down to the Virginia Tidewater Wednesday.
And those persistent winds are piled up water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding was reported from parts of the Jersey Shore to southeast Virginia during Wednesday's morning and evening high tides.
Flooding was reported Wednesday morning in downtown Norfolk, Smithfield and Suffolk, Virginia, according to the National Weather Service.
Widespread gusts of 30-45 mph were ongoing as of Thursday evening, with peak gusts over 45 mph reported along the coast of North Carolina.
Those persistent winds were piling up water from the ocean and bays along parts of the coast. Water levels reached major flood stage during high tide Thursday evening.
A 16-mile stretch of the North Carolina Highway 12 on the Outer Banks is closed in both directions due to ocean overwash. Specifically, the road is closed from Sea Oats Drive to Oregon Inlet Road in Dare County.
Rising waters forced the cancellation of the Oceans Calling festival in Maryland.
You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria for a nor’easter are met more often than you would think.
A nor’easter simply means that the winds blow into an area from the northeast. For the Northeast, that usually means an area of low pressure is just off the coast, which brings the winds in this direction.
(More: What is a nor’easter? )
Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters and that is because nor’easters do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.
The most notable nor’easters tend to bring heavy snow because these lows move up along the Gulf Stream, tapping into the warm ocean. This warm, moist air then clashes with the cold air over the Northeast to create heavy snowfall. Fortunately, this one is occurring way earlier, so it is all rain this time.

President Trump touted Thursday's long-awaited state dinner at the White House as a tough ticket, and while the Chinese business delegation was notably absent , the glittering event featured a wide array of US CEOs.
The official invite list included more than 30 present or former US CEOs, largely from the technology sector, as well as from banking, carmakers, and pharmaceuticals.
Perhaps most striking were the four CEOs whom Trump's team chose to sit at the head table with the two heads of state.
Elon Musk of Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) was seated next to Melania Trump, while Jensen Huang of Nvidia ( NVDA ), former Apple ( AAPL ) CEO Tim Cook, as well as Lisa Su of Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) filled out the head table.
In his remarks before the crowd, Trump said the US and Chinese relationship has been built on a "foundation of commerce and mutual respect between our countries, and together we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
The dinner menu, according to the White House, featured three courses to showcase "American ingredients with subtle Chinese influence," including a wild mushroom fricassée, sesame-crusted sea bass, and honey ice cream.
Read more: Tech stocks gain after tech titan dinner with Trump and China's Xi Jinping
The guest list was notable for the outsized presence of tech CEOs and leaders in artificial intelligence. Huang, in particular, has spoken out in recent days against government regulations on the sector, a position Trump has often echoed.
One of the attendees, Satya Nadella of Microsoft, spoke to Yahoo Finance's Deirdre Bosa earlier this week and offered optimism about the overall US-China relationship, saying of AI, "I think both sides will care about the same set of things at the end of the day, which is they want to be able to have this technology actually help their citizens get value." He said safety will be an important element for both sides as norms are set.
The dinner — like many previous Trump events — mixed CEOs among administration officials, Republican party leaders, Fox News hosts, and Supreme Court justices.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio was at a nearby table, seated next to Citigroup ( C ) CEO Jane Fraser. Former Amazon ( AMZN ) CEO Jeff Bezos was seated next to Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, according to a photo.

articles.title_orig: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.title_zh: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.content_orig:
One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.
Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.
Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.
The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.
In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".
"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."
An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".
"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.
Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.
Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.
Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

iOS 27 adds a variety of new features and changes for Apple Wallet, including one that’s been on my wishlist for years: the ability to import physical passes.
Apple Wallet offers a host of features to help you replace your physical wallet and keys.
It holds credit cards, driver’s licenses, transit cards, boarding passes, event tickets, car keys, home keys, hotel keys, and more.
And with iOS 27, the Wallet app takes another big step toward being the only wallet you need.
That’s because you can now import physical passes, tickets, membership cards, and the like into Apple Wallet.
Here’s how it works, per Apple :
iPhone and Apple Watch users will be able to create and store passes in Apple Wallet from physical cards, like loyalty or membership cards, eliminating the need to fumble through pockets and bags. With Siri mode in the Camera app, users simply point their iPhone at any physical card with a barcode or even screenshot a digital one, and they’ll be prompted to save it to Apple Wallet. Users can also create and add a pass directly from Apple Wallet. Once added, passes are ready to present as a barcode or QR code right from their iPhone or Apple Watch.
Digital passes are a lot more common today than when Apple Wallet first launched. But they aren’t available for everything.
I definitely still encounter businesses and events that utilize physical passes exclusively. And when I do, it adds a little anxiety to my life because I then need to remember to bring those passes with me at the right time.
But with iOS 27, everything can start going in the Wallet app, which is always with me. By putting everything in Wallet, the mental burden of remembering to bring something extra is suddenly gone.

articles.title_zh: Taylor Swift issues brutal warning about toxic ex in scathing ‘Patient Zero’ lyrics
articles.content_orig:
Taylor Swift’s latest lyrics are better than revenge.
The pop star issued a brutal warning about a toxic ex in her new song “Patient Zero” — and fans believe she was referring to former flame Joe Jonas, despite the singer claiming it was inspired by a friend’s situation.
In the new track off “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore,” out Friday, Swift sings about befriending her ex’s new girlfriend.
She describes herself as “patient zero” — meaning she was the first to experience the emotional damage caused by the unnamed partner’s love and manipulation — and recalls the new girlfriend confiding in her about the couple’s issues.
“If you wanna party with somebody who might know / About the devil on his shoulder under his halo / When the toxins take their hold, you’d rather die than let it go / But if you’re sick of him, I got you, I was patient zero,” she sings.
Many Swifties took to social media to claim the situation was reminiscent to Swift’s real-life dynamic with Joe Jonas and his now-ex-wife, Sophie Turner.
The Grammy winner briefly dated Jonas in 2008 before he, infamously, dumped her in a 27-second phone call.
Jonas began dating Turner in 2016, and in 2019, she and Swift seemed to become friendly, making several public appearances together.
However, it was the “Game of Thrones” alum’s 2023 separation from Jonas that brought her and the songwriter especially close.
Swift, notably, offered Turner her New York City apartment as a free, safe space for the actress and her two daughters during her custody and divorce battle with Jonas.
Due to this situation, many Swifties shared their theory that Swift believes she was Jonas’ “patient zero” and ultimately supported Turner because of it.
“so my patient zero theory is that she wrote this song for Sophie Turner amidst her very public divorce with Joe Jonas,” one theorized on X . “Joe & Taylor were each other’s first public romances, making her ‘patient zero.’ She heard the rumors about their breakup, & wasn’t surprised when sophie called.”
“I mean Sophie literally moved into her house lol 💯 it’s Sophie/Joe,” another added .
A third wrote , “Probably not about this but patient zero REALLY reminds me of when she and sophie turner became thick as thieves when her and joe jonas broke up.”
Others, however, are convinced Swift is singing about Joe Alwyn, who Swift dated for more than six years .
Many fans came to this conclusion by comparing “Patient Zero” to other songs Swift previously wrote about the “Hamnet” star.
In her 2019 track “Cruel Summer” — widely believed to be about the beginning of their love story — Swift invoked imagery of a devilish guy she fell for in the song’s pre-chorus.
Similarly, the songwriter compared the subject of “Patient Zero” to an angelic-looking devil with the line about her knowing about “the devil on his shoulder under his halo.”
Additionally, her 2022 song “You’re Losing Me,” which is interpreted as being about the slow breakdown of her relationship with the British actor, also featured a medical theme like “Patient Zero,” with a pulse in the background of the track.
Swift, however, shared the song’s inspiration with Capital FM on Friday, saying, “I was hanging out with a bunch of friends, and one of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy.
“Everyone in our group just immediately started saying like, ‘Oh, I’ve been through that too’, and telling the stories of when this kind of reach out had happened for them,” she continued.
Reps for Swift, Jonas and Alwyn did not immediately respond to Page Six’s requests for comment.

Joe Giudice is asking the public to have compassion for his daughter Milania Giudice after her recent airport incident.
In an exclusive statement to Page Six, the former “Real Housewives of New Jersey” star revealed Milania, 20, has been struggling privately with the loss of a close friend and the pressures of growing up in the public eye.
“Milania is a good girl. She has a big heart, she loves deeply, and she cares enormously about the people in her life,” Joe, 54, said. “She is also young and going through a very difficult period right now.”
Joe said the death of Milania’s close friend Victoria Zardoya in July “affected” his daughter “tremendously,” adding that she has been trying to process the loss while dealing with life in the spotlight.
“Losing someone you love is incredibly painful, and grief does not have a timeline,” he said. “She has been trying to process that loss while also dealing with the pressures that come with growing up in the public eye.”
Joe also cautioned against judging Milania based on a single moment, saying, “I know my daughter. I know her heart, and I know that what people may see from the outside does not tell the whole story of what someone is experiencing privately.
“There have been difficult moments, but those moments do not define who Milania is as a person.”
Joe, who is represented by Dominton Talent House, added, “I love my daughter, and I will always stand beside her.”
His comments come after Milania was captured in a since-deleted video getting into a heated exchange with her mother, Teresa Giudice, 54, and older sister, Gia Giudice, 25, at an airport while surrounded by police.
In the clip, Milania repeatedly asked, “This is what we do now?” as Teresa told her, “I love you.” Gia then told her mother to “let her do what she wants to do” before Milania snapped at Teresa, saying “Shut the f–k up!”
The video offered little context for what prompted the confrontation, but an incident report obtained by Page Six explained that Milania was “having suicidal thoughts” and a “mental breakdown” at Tampa International Airport in Florida on Wednesday.
Cops were notified that “multiple females need police ASAP,” that Milania “got away” from her family and that she had been separated from a counselor who was traveling with them.
Milania was located about 10 minutes later and was escorted to her gate by police. There was no arrest or medical transport.

Milania had just been “released” from a nearby hospital, according to law enforcement sources who spoke to US Sun .
The airport incident came after Milania was arrested in New Jersey on a simple assault charge stemming from a domestic dispute at her mother’s home on May 14.
According to a police report, Milania was “throwing food [and] candles” during the dispute, while her sister Gabriella Giudice called 911 and reported that she was “acting erratically.” No weapons or injuries were reported. A judge later alleged during Milania’s arraignment that she struck the alleged victim , identified only as “LR,” in the head with her fist, causing redness to the person’s forehead. Milania pleaded not guilty.
She subsequently enrolled in anger management classes as part of the ongoing case. In August, her attorney told a judge they were postponing her hearing so she could complete the course.
For Joe, however, the focus is supporting his daughter as she works through what he described as an especially painful chapter.
“As her father, my priority is making sure my daughter knows that she is loved and supported,” he said. “Our family is doing everything we can to be there for her and give her the support and space she needs right now.”

articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia intercepts wave of Houthi missiles as oil climbs to one-week high
articles.content_orig:
The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, the main alternative route for Saudi oil
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, with the latest attacks pushing oil prices ⁠to a one-week high over fears of spiralling supply disruptions.
The ⁠Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said the missiles were ⁠aimed at Taif in western Saudi ​Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, with the Houthis claiming their attacks were aimed at “a sensitive target” in the capital Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu.
Oil prices climbed about 3%, but trade was volatile and prices came off session highs after reports the US and Iran discussed reopening the strait of Hormuz .
The escalating attacks threaten Saudi Arabia’s ⁠ability to export oil through the Red Sea at a time when the strait of Hormuz is disrupted and the kingdom’s east-west pipeline is only now resuming operations after drone strikes earlier ​this month . The Houthis declared a naval blockade on the kingdom in July, opening a ‌second theatre in the US-Iran war.
It was ‌not clear whether there was any damage or casualties in either Taif or Yanbu, the main alternative route for Saudi oil.
The Houthis seized the whole Yemeni western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab el-Mandeb waterway.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government pressed world leaders on Thursday for help defeating the militants, saying that their new perch along one of the world’s busiest waterways presents an international economic risk.
While claiming that their blockade only applies to Saudi shipping and there remains no threat to commercial shipping on the Red Sea, the Houths have also warned other nations not to get involved.
But the vice-president of the internationally recognised government council urged world leaders at the UN general assembly not to trust the Houthis’ assurances – and to see a bigger picture in the crisis around the strait.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” said vice-president, Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer.
Arguing that protecting the strait “is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation,” he urged the international community to keep weapons and technology from getting into the rebels’ hands.
The Saudi-backed government’s forces had earlier repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to Yemen’s third-biggest city Taiz from the southern port city of Aden where the internationally recognised administration is based, government sources said.
The Houthis ⁠have kept up pressure along a steep, winding mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd, a lifeline for government forces and the ​only route for goods and residents to reach Taiz and travel ​abroad. Seizing parts of the road could allow the Houthis to ​tighten their grip around the city and deal another blow to the government, which has struggled to regain the initiative since losing the western coast.
Riyadh’s foreign ministry said on Friday that Saudi ⁠Arabia, Turkey and ⁠Pakistan would ⁠hold ​an urgent ⁠meeting of their chiefs ⁠of ​staff ‌to ‌discuss ways to ‌support repel the Houthi attacks under their joint ‌defence agreement. Under the defence pact, all three countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three.
Officials in Pakistan are said to be deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East.

articles.title_orig: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.title_zh: ‘We are hemorrhaging’: Cracks emerge in GOP’s Florida firewall
articles.content_orig:
Fox News Digital spoke to Donalds about his tightening race for Florida governor against Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican.
Florida gubernatorial candidate, Republican Congressman Byron Donalds , is taking aim at his Democratic opponent David Jolly over his shifting political positions and party affiliation, in a contest that is resurfacing themes from the 2016 congressional race between Jolly and Charlie Crist.
"You were pro-choice, then you were pro-life, then you were pro-choice. It was only after you switched parties that you switched your position. This was not a matter of conviction for you; it was for political convenience," Jolly said about Charlie Crist when Jolly was a Republican running against Crist, a Democrat, for Congress in 2016.
Ten years later, Jolly is now a Democrat running for Florida governor and facing the same criticism for allegedly changing his positions for political gain, this time, in his race for governor against Donalds.
"The shift in positions by David Jolly is not because of personal conviction, it is purely because of political convenience," Donalds told Fox News Digital, referencing that 2016 exchange.
DESANTIS ENDORSES FLORIDA GOP SLATE INCLUDING BYRON DONALDS IN GOVERNOR'S RACE
Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., takes aim at gubernatorial opponent David Jolly's decades-long history of changing parties and political positions in an interview with Fox News Digital. (Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images ; Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Some of the shifts in Jolly’s positions include issues like abortion, immigration and drilling off the coast of Florida.
As a Republican, Jolly said he believed "life begins at conception," authored legislation to defund Planned Parenthood and co-sponsored fetal-personhood legislation. He also voted for a federal 20-week abortion ban. Now running as a Democrat, Jolly calls himself "pro-choice," supports codifying the Roe v. Wade framework and says he would veto legislation restricting abortion access as governor.
Jolly’s immigration views have also shifted sharply as he attempts to run for governor in a state that voted for Trump each of the last three presidential cycles by wide margins, with many voters motivated by Trump’s immigration policies.
As a Republican, he campaigned on securing the border, supported tighter screening for Syrian and Iraqi refugees and voted for the American SAFE Act. Today, he says the country should have "wide gates" for people coming to work or seek asylum, argues that crossing the border without legal status should not necessarily be treated as a crime in those circumstances and has called the Republican link between immigration and crime "gross," "immoral" and "wrong."
As voters consistently say that affordability is a top-of-mind concern, Donalds is also hitting Jolly’s record on healthcare as an example of inconsistency that shows a lack of credibility on the issue.
NEVER-TRUMP REPUBLICAN IS TOP DEM CHOICE IN CRUCIAL FLORIDA PRIMARY
Former Republican Representative David Jolly, Democratic gubernatorial candidate for Florida, speaks during the National Action Network (NAN) 35th Anniversary Convention in New York on Thursday, April 9, 2026. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"When David Jolly was in Congress, he opposed Obamacare," Donalds said. "Now trying to run for governor, he wants to expand Obamacare in Florida. I mean, these are just some of the complete shifts that we've seen in what he stands for."
Another issue Donalds is taking issue with involves the period after the devastating Deepwater Horizon oil spill, which sent oil and tar balls washing ashore along roughly 178 miles of Florida coastline, contributed to an estimated loss of 1.88 million planned recreational visits in northwest Florida and cost the region $1.3 billion in visitor spending, $2.04 billion in economic output and more than 20,000 job-years.
Within a year of the spill, Jolly’s lobbying firm represented a client that publicly advocated for legislation that could have expanded offshore drilling in the Gulf of Mexico. Three Bridges Advisors listed H.R. 909, the Roadmap for America’s Energy Future, among the subjects of its 2011 lobbying activity for the Free Enterprise Nation, which supported the bill. Jolly also wrote a post on the group’s website stating that Free Enterprise Nation was "advocating for" the legislation.
BYRON DONALDS SHUTS DOWN BILL MAHER’S CLAIM ON GOP PRIMARY RACISM, SAYS 'FLORIDA IS A MERITOCRACY'
Rep. Byron Donalds, a Republican from Florida and gubernatorial candidate, won Florida's Republican primary for governor on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Orlando, Fla., easily fending off challengers after receiving an early endorsement from President Donald Trump. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Jolly said he had "never lobbied for offshore drilling," but PolitiFact rated that claim "Mostly False" after finding that Jolly acknowledged attending a meeting where the bill was discussed, which lobbying experts said technically counted as lobbying.
Donalds cited the controversy to Fox News Digital saying, "Deepwater Horizon exploded in the Gulf of America, David Jolly went and became a lobbyist for more oil drilling off the coast of Florida, that is a fact and so, what we're seeing is a history of somebody who does everything possible, will say whatever, will be paid by whomever that are only in the interest of David Jolly."
With polls showing a tightening race, the RealClearPolitics average gives Donalds a nearly 4-point lead. The candidates are also sparring over debate scheduling: Donalds has agreed to three proposed debates, while Jolly, who previously accepted two other debate invitations, has now ruled out participating in debates this cycle.
"Now he's ducking debates," Donalds told Fox News Digital. "He won't debate me because he knows that on a debate stage, I will hold him accountable for these things."

Jolly has hit Donalds on the campaign trail on a variety of issues as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in Florida since Lawton Chiles won re-election in 1994. Primarily, Jolly has focused on data centers and labeled Donalds as a candidate more interested in partisan culture-war battles than addressing Florida’s rising housing, insurance and healthcare costs.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Jolly campaign for comment.
Donalds told Fox News Digital that Jolly’s flips on both party registration and the issues are things his campaign will continue to focus on.
"What you find with David Jolly is somebody who's done a complete 180 simply to run for office again and to gain relevance again and the people of Florida simply cannot trust David Jolly because we cannot afford David Jolly’s flip-flopping when it comes to the great state of Florida," Donalds said.

articles.title_orig: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
articles.title_zh: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
articles.content_orig:
Danish intelligence officials have warned that Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, on Thursday identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it wrote in a report.
"The purpose would be to redirect European resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response."
The DDIS added that it saw no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a NATO country, although it said it could not rule this out.
Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops, possibly without national insignia, into NATO countries on its border, the DDIS said. However, it said that such a buildup would be difficult to conceal and take several months to prepare.
The new threat assessment joins a chorus of Russia warnings from top European security officials and lawmakers in recent days.
NATO members that border Russia are Finland, Norway and Poland as well as the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Poland's government on Thursday said a blaze at a Starlink ground station in the country was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.
Poland's deputy prime minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, said it had not yet been established who was responsible for the fire, but "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack," according to Reuters .
A spokesperson for Russia's embassy in London was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC. The Kremlin has previously denied involvement in similar incidents.
Denmark's intelligence service also warned that Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more attacks against the West and NATO, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past."
These could include major cyberattacks that seriously damage vital societal functions as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, the DDIS said.

articles.title_orig: Telecoms networks disrupted in Tigray as Ethiopia's military cites major losses by rebels
articles.title_zh: Telecoms networks disrupted in Tigray as Ethiopia's military cites major losses by rebels
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four years ago, a peace deal ended the brutal war in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, one of the deadliest conflicts of the 21st century. Now, the violence has returned — but the battle lines have changed.
Tigrayan rebels are again fighting the federal government, while forces that were once enemies are now fighting side by side.
On Wednesday, Tigrayan forces seized three airports controlled by the federal government, while fighting also broke out in the neighboring regions of Amhara and Afar.
The hostilities have shattered the 2022 peace agreement that ended a war estimated to have killed around 600,000 people . Relations between the federal government and Tigray’s leaders had been worsening for months.
It’s unclear what led to the recent fighting, with both sides offering conflicting accounts.
Tigray’s regional government said federal forces attacked first and that it ordered its forces to respond, calling it a “defensive war.” While Getachew Reda, an adviser to Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said the TPLF had launched an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Afar and Amhara and seized the three airports in Tigray, accusing it of taking “irresponsibility to new heights.”
The renewed violence this week follows almost two months of smaller clashes. The nongovernmental organization Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) says fighting between Tigrayan and federal forces began near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan on August 1. The two sides also accused each other of starting those clashes.
According to ACLED, federal drone strikes and Tigrayan troop deployments followed, with Tigrayan forces moving tanks and artillery south this month.
National carrier Ethiopian Airlines has suspended all flights to Tigray after the airport seizures.
The TPLF was once Ethiopia’s most powerful political force. It dominated the coalition that governed the country for nearly three decades, despite Tigrayans making up a relatively small share of Ethiopia’s population.
That changed after Abiy became prime minister in 2018 following years of anti-government protests. He introduced political reforms and made peace with neighboring Eritrea, which won him the Nobel Peace Prize a year later.
But relations with the TPLF deteriorated. Abiy replaced the old ruling coalition with his Prosperity Party in 2019; the TPLF refused to join.
‘Practically this has been a genocide’
After national elections were postponed during the Covid-19 pandemic, Tigray held its own regional vote despite objections from Addis Ababa.
In November 2020, Tigrayan forces attacked federal military bases in the region. Abiy sent troops in, and Eritrean forces and fighters from Amhara later fought alongside the federal army.
By the time the war ended two years later, millions of people had been displaced and parts of Tigray had been pushed into famine. Both sides faced accusations of serious human rights abuses.
Hostilities came to an end when the federal government and TPLF signed an African Union-brokered agreement in Pretoria, South Africa, on November 2, 2022.
Under the deal, Tigrayan forces were to disarm and federal authority would return to the region. Humanitarian aid and basic services would resume, and an interim administration was later set up to govern Tigray until elections.
But major disputes remained, including over territory claimed by both Tigray and Amhara and the return of people displaced by the war. Meanwhile, Eritrea, whose soldiers had fought alongside federal forces, was not party to the agreement.
“The agreement didn’t collapse overnight — it was systematically hollowed out over three years,” Surafel Getahun, an Ethiopian geopolitics researcher, told CNN.
Getahun said both sides bore responsibility. He accused the federal government of failing to fulfill key parts of the agreement, including returning displaced people, and the TPLF of breaching it by retaking control of the regional administration and rebuilding its military forces.
The TPLF was also divided by an internal power struggle , which further weakened the peace process. Rival factions emerged around TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael and Reda, the head of the Tigray interim administration who had been a senior TPLF figure. Reda was later expelled from the party by Gebremichael’s faction, and Abiy appointed a new interim leader in April 2025.
A month later, Gebremichael’s faction took back control of Tigray’s government . It restored the regional legislature that existed before the war and installed Gebremichael as regional president.
On Sunday, the TPLF joined six other armed groups in a new alliance seeking to remove Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration. The alliance includes former enemies who fought on opposite sides of the last war.
TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom told the Associated Press the groups would cooperate politically and militarily. Asked whether joining the alliance violated the Pretoria agreement, Asgedom said the accord was “no longer valid.”
The Amhara Fano National Movement fought alongside the federal government against the TPLF during the last war, then turned against it in 2023. The Oromo Liberation Army, which has long fought Abiy’s government in Oromia, is also a member.
Reuters reported Wednesday that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside the Fano group in Amhara and a local armed group in Afar.
But Getahun questioned how long the alliance would hold.
The TPLF and Fano remain divided over contested territory, particularly Western Tigray, and its members have different political and military goals.
“This is a temporary marriage of convenience against a mutual enemy rather than a lasting political agreement,” he said.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters on Monday that the groups had already been working together with financial backing from Eritrea. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated since their forces fought together in the last war, though the Eritrean government has repeatedly denied supporting Ethiopian armed groups.
The African Union (AU) said Wednesday that the airport seizures were inconsistent with the Pretoria deal and urged both parties to de-escalate. It also asked for help from former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 agreement.
Tigray has yet to recover from the last war, with communities still rebuilding and many displaced people still unable to return home.
Ethiopia is already dealing with armed conflicts in Amhara and Oromia, and ACLED says the federal military was “stretched” before the renewed fighting with the TPLF. But the armed groups in the new alliance vary in their fighting capacity, with several lacking the organization or recruits for wider operations and others largely confined to local areas, according to the conflict monitor.
There is also the risk of Eritrea’s military becoming involved. Tensions have grown between the two countries over Ethiopia’s push for access to the Red Sea , including through Eritrea’s port of Assab. The AU urged Ethiopia’s neighbors to avoid actions that could fuel the conflict.
The region is already grappling with the war in Sudan and longstanding tensions between Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan over the Nile.
Getahun warned that the current fighting could become even more devastating than the previous conflict.
“A renewed war would likely end up far bloodier and more widespread than the 2020–2022 fighting,” he said.
“Immediate de-escalation and dialogue” are now essential, he added, arguing that negotiations remain “the only viable path forward.”
