articles.title_orig: Benjamin Netanyahu attacks Israel’s enemies and allies in UN speech
articles.title_zh: Benjamin Netanyahu attacks Israel’s enemies and allies in UN speech
articles.content_orig:
Delegates walk out of Netanyahu’s UN speech
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used his platform at the United Nations General Assembly to attack detractors and allies alike, and his presence sparked uproar in the chamber.
Speaking before the UNGA on Thursday, Netanyahu attacked New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, critics and Iran’s leadership, as well as allied countries like the United Kingdom, Turkiye and France.
Back home, the prime minister is locked in a tight race to stay in power ahead of an October 27 election, and analysts say his UNGA speech was aimed as much at people back home as it was at international viewers.
Dozens of envoys from around the world walked out as the speech began, some jeering and booing, while Netanyahu’s own team stood and applauded, and the speaker of the session shouted for order.
“If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t left this hall, please do so now,” Netanyahu said to those turning their backs on him.
He addressed the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran in February, saying: “Devastating Iran’s nuclear facilities was hard, was very hard to do.”
“But for me, it was one of the easiest decisions I’ve ever had to make as prime minister”, claiming that if he had not, “we’d all be dead”, he added.
In his own speech before the UNGA on Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also addressed the nuclear issue and called out the “double standard”.
“The nuclear weapon is in Israel, but the inspectors are in Iran. Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions,” Pezeshkian said.
Netanyahu on Thursday said that Israel was fighting a “seven-front war”, including Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Syria, Lebanon, Iran, Yemen’s Houthis and militias in Iraq.
“We are going to win. We have no other choice,” Netanyahu declared, repeating the words of his older brother Yonatan Netanyahu, who was killed in 1976 during Operation Entebbe in Uganda.
In his speech, Netanyahu targeted Turkiye and its President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, among others, accusing Ankara of being a “spreader of anti-Semitic lies”.
The Turkish presidency responded with a statement saying that Netanyahu’s use of the UN platform to attack Erdogan was “incompatible with the ideals of peace, the rule of law and dialogue that the United Nations represents”. It pointed to the International Criminal Court’s arrest warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
“Netanyahu’s outrageous and despicable remarks targeting President Erdogan cannot obscure his massacres, the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza or the legal proceedings against him under international law,” Presidential Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said in a statement posted on X.
The Turkish president addressed the UNGA himself on Tuesday, saying Israel’s actions reflected a “genocidal mindset” and “state terrorism”, and that Gaza had become “the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time”.
The United Kingdom and France, historic partners of Israel, were also in Netanyahu’s firing line. They have become increasingly outspoken in their criticism of the country’s actions and have both imposed limited sanctions on Israeli exports from the occupied West Bank.
“They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he said.
But Netanyahu thanked his “friend”, United States President Donald Trump.
“In this battle against the barbarians, we’ve had no greater partner than President Trump,” he said, as the US delegation joined the Israeli one in applauding Netanyahu’s remark.
“I thank him,” said Netanyahu, adding that Israel and the US had acted together as pilots from both countries “flew joint missions over the skies of Iran”.
Netanyahu said the US and Israel also “worked together to bring back our remaining hostages [from Gaza]”, as he defended Israeli actions in the enclave against charges of genocide.
“To all those spreading lies about my country, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the anti-Semitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you,” Netanyahu said as he attacked Zohran Mamdani, who had previously said he would push for the arrest of the Israeli prime minister during his visit to the city.
“Mr Mamdani, you tried to stop me from coming here. You tried to silence me. Well, you can’t silence me,” Netanyahu said as he denied that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.
Reacting to Netanyahu’s comments, Mamdani called the accusations against him “baseless lies” meant to “sanitise his genocide of Palestinians”.
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide in Gaza, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court (ICC) said in 2024 it had reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu was responsible for war crimes in Gaza, where over 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Netanyahu denies the ICC charges.
Netanyahu attended the UNGA meeting despite an ICC warrant calling for his arrest. While he was welcomed, the Trump administration denied a visa for Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, who addressed the UNGA through a prerecorded video statement from Ramallah earlier in the day.
As Netanyahu spoke, activists from US-based organisation Jewish Voice for Peace protested outside, accusing the United Nations of “playing host to a war criminal”.
“All across New York, Jews, Palestinians and people of conscience are rising up to demand an end to US support for the livestreamed horrors, rigged ceasefires and forever wars,” Sonya Meyerson-Knox, the group’s communications director, told Al Jazeera.
Meyerson-Knox said that “solidarity with Palestinian freedom has never been greater, and here in the US we are demanding with one voice to stop arming Israel”.
Adding to tensions, dozens of protesters, some brandishing “stop the genocide” banners, gathered near the UN. Several demonstrators were detained, including prominent actor Susan Sarandon.
Inside the UN, but addressing divisions back home in Israel, Netanyahu said: “Throughout this long war, our goal never wavers – to win with unwavering resolve … What unites us is so much stronger: our history, our values, our courage.”
Ariel Cohen, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center, said the Israeli prime minister delivered a “good speech” at the UNGA but that he did so in the “wrong forum”.
“That speech should be given at an election rally in Israel; this is who he’s communicating to,” Cohen told Al Jazeera. “He is making points that should be made to the Israeli audience for his political survival.”
Netanyahu is only making a whirlwind stop in New York before rushing back to Israel, where the election campaign is in full swing. He is not scheduled to meet any top US leaders.

articles.title_orig: New Jersey’s governor calls on her lieutenant governor to resign over ethics report
articles.title_zh: New Jersey’s governor calls on her lieutenant governor to resign over ethics report
articles.content_orig:
New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill said Thursday evening that she gave Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell “until tomorrow” to resign after an investigation found he had violated state ethics and harassment policy.
“Today, I’m announcing the conclusion and findings of an independent investigation into allegations regarding Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell,” Sherrill wrote on X . “The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office. I’m calling for his resignation and giving him until tomorrow to do so.”
The state said this month that it had hired a law firm to investigate allegations against Caldwell, a Democrat who was elected on the ticket with Sherrill last year , claiming that he had behaved inappropriately toward women.
Sherrill said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses persisted despite multiple warnings and trainings.”
“The substantiated finding of sexual harassment is extremely troubling. I’ve seen firsthand how a hostile culture can undermine everyone’s ability to succeed. It’s insidious and ruptures the trust within an organization,” she said.
Sherrill said that the investigation “fully examined the evidence, followed the facts, and protected everyone’s privacy” and that Caldwell’s resignation “is necessary and in the best interest of New Jersey residents.”
Lawyers for Caldwell, who has denied the allegations, said in a statement Thursday night that they “strongly disputed the three findings in the investigation,” as its conclusions “go further than the evidence supports.”
“This unnecessarily protracted and one-sided process lacked the requisite due process that should be afforded every citizen of this state,” said Thomas Calcagni, a lawyer for Caldwell.
Calcagni said Caldwell was “not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations or offer readily identifiable witnesses who possessed more pertinent, first-hand knowledge of the events in question.”
The 61-page report found that Caldwell sexually harassed a young female staffer and her friend. Caldwell was also found to have violated state ethics rules for using his office to try to promote a state employee whom he had a romantic relationship with “on multiple occasions,” without disclosing the relationship.
He also violated ethics rules by making a practice of taking personal guests to ticketed events without providing payment or reimbursement for the tickets, the report said.
State Senate Republican Leader Anthony M. Bucco said in a statement Thursday that the investigation’s findings were “deeply disappointing.”
“This situation has gone on for far too long, and if he doesn’t agree to resign, the Legislature should follow the necessary protocols to resolve this matter once and for all,” Bucco said.
Caldwell is only the fourth lieutenant governor in New Jersey history, as the role was established by referendum in 2005. It includes the responsibility of taking over as governor when the governor is away, which Caldwell has done numerous times since the investigation began.
Caldwell is also New Jersey’s secretary of state, overseeing elections, a critical role as the midterm elections approach in November.

articles.title_orig: The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: A Printable List
articles.title_zh: The 100 Best TV Shows of the 21st Century: A Printable List
articles.content_orig:
The New York Times ‘ exhaustive list of the best TV shows of the 21st century traces its origin to a similar list of the best books a couple years ago. The idea, Times canon editor Gilbert Cruz tells The Hollywood Reporter , was to reach out to the world’s best authors (many of them he notes, already write for the Times or the Times Book Review in one capacity or another), and have them select their favorites.
“It was such a success that we said, let’s try it again with movies,” says Cruz. Celebrities, however, are a different beast than authors, though the Times figured it out.
For the TV list, Cruz said that they reached out to more than 1,000 people, and about 500 or so ended up participating. Many of them also agreed to discuss their picks on camera, with videos interwoven throughout the list.
“Part of the thing that we’re promising readers is we’re doing this because these are people in these industries — the book industry, the movie industry, TV industry — who know about this stuff, create this stuff, but also care about this stuff,” says Cruz. “When you hear creators, showrunners, stars talking about the things that they love to see, yes, they are famous people, but also they’re just TV fans like the rest of us, right?
“Maybe you could do it in audio as well, and it would deliver some of that, but you wouldn’t go as far as you can with video, where you can hear Connie Britton telling a funny story like, ‘oh, I passed on Arrested Development because I thought it was dumb as hell,’ and then to see the final product, it’s not only the sound of her voice telling that story, but it’s the look on her face telling that story. In the end, what we wanted to do was just show people that TV creators love this medium just like we do, and that’s why we asked them to participate in this project.”
Earlier this summer Cruz was named “canon editor” at the Times , a role that immediately raised some eyebrows in media circles? What even is a canon in the context of an institution like the Times ?
The TV list is in many ways the textbook example of what Cruz hopes to bring to the table, building on the learnings from the books and films list that were previously published.
“The idea is, can you have someone and a small team that can make a franchise out of this, make it into something that is living on a more regular basis, but also is interconnected,” says Cruz. “You don’t necessarily want all these things sort of popping up all over the newsroom on their own in their various silos.”
“It’s brand new, it’s an experiment,” he adds. “I’m still figuring out what the heck it is, and a big part of it is can we leverage our access to amplify our authority in all of these spaces — books, movies, TV — The New York Times has access, and we’ve always had access. In all of these places, we’ve had authority, and we’ve always had authority.”
The TV list, of course, is just the start. Others will follow, with video and dynamic features intertwined with the critical takes and the written word. Though just how many of these projects Cruz and his team (when he has hired his team) do remains to be determined.
“We need to figure out what the right cadence is. You know, it [the same list] can’t be every year. Obviously, that wouldn’t work,” he says. “That would be too big of a heave, and you wouldn’t get enough variance in the list every year in order to make it meaningful.
“Part of my challenge, and it is a challenge, is to figure out how to make sure, as you say, that these are not just one-offs,” he adds. “That it’s not just ‘here’s this thing we put out in September 2026, maybe you’ll never hear about it again.” Is there a way to sort of make them live on a more regular basis, even the ones we’ve already published?”

articles.title_orig: R&B Singer Attacks Trump for Using Hit Song in Campaign Ad
articles.title_zh: R&B Singer Attacks Trump for Using Hit Song in Campaign Ad
articles.content_orig:
R&B singer JMSN is blasting Donald Trump for using his song “Love Me,” in a bizarre new ad glorifying the president.
Trump is also drawing scrutiny for using taxpayer dollars to produce the ad, which blares “Love Me” while touting his policies, despite a federal ban on spending public money for political promotion.
The 30-second ad, which debuted this week on right-wing news outlets, features a portion of JMSN’s song with a chorus singing “I’ll make them love me” over and over against a montage of the 80-year-old president.
“America will never be a communist country,” Trump says in the short spot, before UFC CEO Dana White gushes over the president: “He is the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met, and nothing was going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country he loves.”
The ad also rattles off a list of Trump’s supposed accomplishments, flashing claims such as “Largest tax cuts in history,” “Reigniting American manufacturing,” and “Defend law and order and police.”
JMSN, whose real name is Christian Berishaj, accused Trump on Instagram of “illegally” using his song in the ad.
He argued that “this could have gone 2 ways.”
“1. The President or his team reach out and ask to license the song, I respond ‘no’ and you never know about it.
“2. The President illegally uses the song without asking but still the public goes full r----d and immediately assumes that a license was.”
“Obviously it went the second way,” the singer wrote.
JMSN, who was born to an Albanian father and grew up in Detroit, Michigan, wrote, “To anybody who has followed my career and knows what I stand for and built my career on, it should go without saying that I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
The indie artist said he doesn’t have a publicist, “so being forced in a situation like this and having to comment is ridiculous,” before declaring, “I am looking at lawyers and handling this internally.”
The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s questions about the ad.
The commercial, which is airing on Fox News and Newsmax just weeks before the midterms, includes a tag reading, “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
But federal law prohibits the use of federal funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes,” including communications that are “purely partisan” and “designed to aid a political party or candidates,” according to The Washington Post .
In a statement to the Post, the White House insisted that the ad is purely a “public service announcement” about “reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic,” the statement claims.
Despite the White House’s claims, the release of the ad came against a clear political backdrop, after Trump told Republicans ahead of the midterms to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said in an X post that the ad could constitute “felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.”
“It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns,” he said.

articles.content_orig:
It’s confirmed: The mysterious Motorola phone getting support for the privacy-focused GrapheneOS will be the Motorola Signature 27 that was announced earlier this week.
GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused take on Android that’s grown popular in recent years, has so far only been available on Pixel devices. That’s for a number of reasons relating back to how Google handles the software and the security components in Pixel (and Tensor) hardware.
But, now, GrapheneOS is officially stepping beyond Pixel and into a device that will come pre-loaded with its version of Android. It was announced that this would be a Motorola device, but which device was left a mystery as all existing Motorola devices were not compatible with the platform.
Unsurprisingly, though, the first GrapheneOS device from Motorola will be the Motorola Signature 27. GrapheneOS confirmed the news on Twitter/X , though other details are still minimal. It’s apparently still planned that devices will be sold with GrapheneOS pre-installed. The Signature 27 was announced earlier this week and its use of the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is likely a major part of the reason it will be able to run GrapheneOS properly.
An exact release date for the Motorola Signature 27 has yet to be confirmed, and it’s unclear if GrapheneOS will be available right away either. It’s already known that future versions of Razr flip and Razr Fold will also support the privacy-focused OS.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.content_orig:
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."
The White House released the invite list for Thursday's state dinner, which includes high-level government officials and several of the world's wealthiest tech executives.
Among the notable people on the guest list are Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet-level officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Mr. Trump's children – Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany – also got invites.
The world's richest person, Elon Musk, is on the list. NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Apple's Tim Cook, Google's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and TikTok investor Jeff Yass also got invites.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also attending. (Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.)
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump walked out of the White House's North Portico shortly after 7 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, then arrived in a car and posed for photos with the Trumps before walking inside.

China is poised to decide which of two Latin American women becomes the first to lead the United Nations, after three rounds of informal voting in the Security Council failed to produce a favourite.
Several UN delegations that spoke to the South China Morning Post over the past three days said Beijing was weighing Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican economist who heads UN Trade and Development, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s ambassador to the UN.
The same delegations said China had ruled out Rafael Grossi, the Argentine director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Grossi is widely seen as Washington’s preferred candidate and was nominated last year by Argentine President Javier Milei.
China has kept cordial but cooler relations with Milei since his 2023 presidential campaign, when he called the Chinese government “assassins” and promised to cut ties in favour of the “civilised side of life”.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

Donald Trump couldn’t help but offer guests at his state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping a first-ever tour of his ballroom construction site.
The president loves to boast to the White House press corps and his Truth Social followers about his passion projects around Washington, D.C ., especially the massive White House ballroom being built. Now, in front of an international audience, Trump has offered to share a glimpse of what he called a “clean and sparkly” construction site.
“And if I could go off script just for a second,” Trump said as dinner guests in the East Room of the White House laughed. “But as a special treat in honor of President Xi and Madame [Liyuan] Peng. I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back.”
“It's one year away from completion — the new ballroom that you've heard about, and you will see something that I think you will really love.”
The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom will fit 650 seats, compared to the 200 seats in the East Room. Trump has said construction will cost about $400 million and that he and other donors would pay for it.
But the project’s contractor told the administration that it would cost $600 million , with at least half expected to be covered by taxpayers, The Washington Post reported in June.
The Trump administration has also been challenged in court over whether it had the authority to tear down the East Wing last October to build the ballroom without Congressional approval. The Supreme Court ruled last month that the president can continue with construction for the time being .
“You'll be the first people to step foot on that, and we'll do that maybe after we're finished with the entertainment tonight. Anybody [who] wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkly, it's our honor to have you do so,” Trump told his dinner guests.
The official delegations from the US and China attended the state dinner. Some notable names on the guest list included first lady Melania Trump , Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio .
Trump was photographed next to Melania while waiting to greet Xi and his wife Peng at the White House ahead of the dinner. Makeup was caked on his left hand, which he often uses to cover up bruising .
The Trump administration has said the black and blue on the back of his hands is due to frequent handshaking and aspirin use .
Several of America’s tech leaders, such as SpaceX’s Elon Musk , OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg , were also in attendance Thursday night amid an AI race with China .
During the legal fight to build his ballroom, Trump argued that it was needed for national security. Underneath the East Wing sits a bunker dating back to 1942, after the U.S. entered World War II. In court filings, the Trump administration noted that bomb shelters, military installations and a medical facility would be added to the bunker during construction.
So when Trump suggested officials from China, an adversary of the U.S., tour the construction site, it raised some eyebrows.
“Of the security bunker? Seems suboptimal,” Reuters journalist Charlie Szymanski wrote on Bluesky.
“Guided tour of the super secure and classified military ballroom for officials of a foreign unfriendly nation. Totally reasonable,” another Bluesky user, Jeff Domingues, posted .
One X user wrote , “Let’s take the leader of China into the ballroom that doubles as a military bunker! Great idea Don!”
Melania led the preparations for the state dinner, which included a menu that the White House said had a “subtle Chinese influence.” For the main course, guests enjoyed sesame-crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy.
Entertainment for the night was headlined by Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at Trump’s second inauguration. Guests were also treated to performances by military ensembles.
“Thank you, Mr. President and Mrs. Trump, for extending to my wife and me your gracious hospitality and thoughtful arrangements,” Xi said at the dinner through an interpreter. “You make us feel truly at home.”
“I would also like to extend my sincere greetings to Americans from all sectors of society who care about China-U.S. relations and support the further growth of our bilateral ties.”

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use expanded database for potential voter purges
articles.content_orig:
The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal voter database, which uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to filter alleged non-citizen voting.
Critics warn the ruling could lead to valid voters being removed from electoral rolls.
The ruling marks a victory for the Trump administration as it seeks to clamp down on allegations of non-citizen voting.
The three liberal-leaning liberals on the Supreme Court dissented from the decision, with the other six conservative justices supporting it. In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.
The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.
The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits. But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using social security numbers.
In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote."
A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.

And City were not easing themselves back into European action either, they went full throttle at the start of a tough set of group games. With Enzo Maresca, it looks like it will be all-out attack to get the best out of this team.
They can look nervous at the back, particularly with the ball at Gianluigi Donnarumma’s feet, but have attacking weapons to hurt any team in this elite competition. This was a performance that their rivals will take note of.

City will certainly scare the traditional heavyweights with Haaland leading their attack and taking an axe to Porto’s defence like he does with logs in his back garden. It was his 58th and 59th goal in 59 games in the Champions League , with his latest an expertly directed header off a post and a calm side-footed finish.

“I didn’t see anything but anyway, you can ask how many times you see me or my bench stand up? Zero, for 95 minutes. How many times do you see their bench? So...” Maresca added.

That includes Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, who was part of a £320m midfield refresh following the departure of Rodri, who was named among the Ballon d’Or nominees a few hours before kick-off to highlight the experience and class City have lost.
Bouaddi, who cost £81.4m from Lille, made a good start in his full debut. The Moroccan teenager is neat on the ball and gets around the pitch, with the next step being able to dominate games like his predecessor.
“In his last game he lost two balls and stayed calm and was back in our box,” Maresca said. “This shows how good he is because any player after two [poor] passes panics, but he is just 18. Erling, Rúben, Mateo [Kovacic], they can manage these kind of games better, but you don’t expect it from a guy of 18. I didn’t see him panic.”
By Bouaddi’s side in midfield was Enzo Fernández, who sought to drive forward into space when City counter-attacked. He was among the players who, along with Dias, were reminded of their Benfica history by the home fans.
Diogo Costa tends to be linked with a move to the Premier League every summer, but has been a one-club man for his career so far. But he showed why clubs are looking at him with his first-half saves to deny Haaland and Rayan Cherki.
Porto’s legendary goalkeeper, Helton, was in the press box at half-time and would have been impressed with the saves, although he was not in his seat when Haaland scored the first goal, which came 94 seconds after the restart.
City had worked the ball around the penalty area, with Antoine Semenyo drawing out Costa before laying off to Fernández. Haaland’s header from the cross had such precision that the goalkeeper did not dive as it angled in off a post.
Still, Porto had their chances with Alberto Costa heading wide from a corner and William Gomes charging down a Donnarumma kick – with City’s most nervous moments coming when they passed around their back line.

“It was an amazing game against the champions of Portugal. We knew it would be a difficult fight, man against man, they are a top team,” Haaland said. “They play amazing football. All the pressure, we have to deliver on the big stage and that’s what we did. We controlled the whole first half, created chances.”
For Maresca, the victory was also a challenge against Porto’s aggression, with the Italian coach adding: “I was very pleased. We know in this kind of game when you come here it’s always difficult or tricky. The environment, the way they grew up, it’s normal, but I think we dealt with that very good.”

articles.title_zh: Ed Sheeran’s weekend Gillette concerts canceled due to arriving nor’easter
articles.content_orig:
Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour.
The concerts scheduled for Friday and Saturday at the New England Patriots home stadium were scrapped because of the upcoming nor’easter , Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the statement said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”
The touring group said that refunds are available and that ticket holders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded.
The announcement comes amid a wider scandal for Sheeran’s “Loop” tour since one of its opening acts was forced out for voicing pro-Palestinian views.
Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour after speaking out in support for the Palestinian people at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Macklemore said he was removed at the behest of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and alleged that Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners.
Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. In a previous statement he said he did not intend to stifle Palestinian support but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium.
Macklemore’s removal prompted Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — to withdraw in protest.
A rep for Sheeran did not immediately return a request for comment. In his first concert since the scandal, Sheeran apologized for the scenario.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
On Thursday, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall.
The multiday nor’easter is expected to hit the East Coast, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island. Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people. Wind gusts are expected to peak on Saturday, reaching up to 60 mph in coastal locations.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.title_zh: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title_zh: China swimmer makes Asian Games history as Thai sprinter wins track 100m
articles.content_orig:
Towering teenager Zhang Zhanshuo became the first swimmer in history to win seven golds at a single Asian Games, while on the track, Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson powered to victory in the 100m.
China’s Zhang, 19, scorched to the men’s 400m freestyle title in the pool in Tokyo on Friday in a Games-record three minutes and 41.28 seconds.
He sat on the lane divider after the race and slowly counted off on his fingers all seven medals he had won.
Zhang also won individual golds in the 200m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, as well as three relays.
He said, after wrapping up a scintillating campaign, that it had been the “perfect week”.
“I think the most important thing is to stay grounded and focused, because the Asian Games are not my ultimate goal,” said Zhang, who stands 198cm (six feet, six inches).
With the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away, China won 30 of the 42 golds in the pool this week.
Their 13-year-old phenomenon Yu Zidi was the undoubted superstar, taking home three individual golds and all in Games-record times.
Not to be outdone, Japan’s 17-year-old Shin Ohashi shattered the men’s 200m breaststroke world record on Thursday.
Swimming, equestrian and diving are taking place in Tokyo, but the city of Nagoya and the wider Aichi prefecture are the main Games host.
The men’s and women’s 100m sprints, the blue riband events in track and field, took place in front of rows of empty seats in Nagoya.
China’s Chen Yujie streaked to a comfortable victory in the women’s final in a Games-record 11.06 seconds.
The men’s was won by 20-year-old Puripol, who burst out of the pack in the final quarter of the race to win in 9.90 seconds, breaking his Games record from earlier in the evening.
It was Thailand’s first men’s 100m gold medal since Suchart Jairsuraparp on home soil at the 1978 Bangkok Games.
On the last evening of gymnastics, Carlos Yulo won the men’s vault for his second gold of the Games.
The double Olympic champion won floor gold on Thursday to complete his collection of major titles.
“I can’t believe it,” the Filipino said.
“In this whole Asian Games, I felt really stressed, but at the same time, I enjoyed what I did today. I really did my part.
“Today was really a miracle for me.”
There’s little time to celebrate, however, with the world championships next month.
South Korea edged China 85-80 in the semifinals of the women’s basketball, and will face hosts Japan for gold.
China had their giant centre Zhang Ziyu, 19, but it was not enough.
Zhang Ziyu stands 223cm (seven feet, four inches) and scored 22 points.
“She was tough to guard,” said South Korea’s Kang Lee-seul.

Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour.
The concerts scheduled for Friday and Saturday at the New England Patriots home stadium were scrapped because of the upcoming nor’easter , Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the statement said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”
The touring group said that refunds are available and that ticket holders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded.
The announcement comes amid a wider scandal for Sheeran’s “Loop” tour since one of its opening acts was forced out for voicing pro-Palestinian views.
Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour after speaking out in support for the Palestinian people at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Macklemore said he was removed at the behest of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and alleged that Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners.
Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. In a previous statement he said he did not intend to stifle Palestinian support but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium.
Macklemore’s removal prompted Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — to withdraw in protest.
A rep for Sheeran did not immediately return a request for comment. In his first concert since the scandal, Sheeran apologized for the scenario.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
On Thursday, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall.
The multiday nor’easter is expected to hit the East Coast, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island. Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people. Wind gusts are expected to peak on Saturday, reaching up to 60 mph in coastal locations.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

'What happened in Israel at Nova music festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain.

“This move is a diplomatic all-timer,” Santi Ruiz, a policy-focused writer for the Institute for Progress and editorial team member at AI company Anthropic, posted on X. “It's like Messi cutting inside. You know it’s coming. It doesn’t matter how many times they run it. You’re getting those pandas, and you’ll like it.”
The tried-and-tested offering came once again on Thursday as Chinese President Xi Jinping announced during his state visit to the U.S. that Ping Ping and Fu Shuang , two giant pandas from a research base in Chengdu, would be lent to Zoo Atlanta in the state of Georgia—but whether this so-called panda diplomacy remains as welcome as it has over the decades is less clear, eliciting mixed reactions in 2026.
The practice gained traction after the National Zoo received giant pandas from Beijing in the wake of President Richard Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon’s historic trip to China in 1972, which marked a new, positive chapter in U.S.-China relations.
China claims ownership of nearly all the giant pandas in the world, even their offspring, and controls who receives them. Beijing eventually shifted from gifting giant pandas to leasing them to other countries in 1984 as the animal’s population dwindled, but the practice continued and spread to other nations like Austria, Canada, and Malaysia. China regularly considers loaning pandas an act of goodwill—even when the host nation typically foots the bill of about $1 million annually for a pair.
A giant panda’s presence or absence in a country tends to represent ebbs and flows of its relationship with China. For instance, amid tensions with Japan over Taiwan , Tokyo returned two giant pandas to Sichuan on loan in January, marking the first time Japan does not have a giant panda since 1972, when China-Japan ties first normalized. In 2010, two U.S.-born panda cubs returned to China , days after Chinese officials warned then-President Barack Obama against meeting the Dalai Lama, whom Beijing considers a separatist.
“No other animal has been turned into a symbol to the extent that pandas have been,” says Czeslaw Tubilewicz, a senior lecturer at Adelaide University.
It’s also no coincidence that Zoo Atlanta received the giant pandas, Tubilewicz says, as the gift represented Beijing’s appreciation of Georgia’s historical economic partnership with China on several aspects: “When most southern states, especially Republican states, turned very negative on China, Georgia continued its pro-China policy consistently. So when it comes to those pandas, and in [Zoo Atlanta], in a way, Xi Jinping is trying to kill two birds with two pandas.”
But China’s transformation from a developing economy to one of the world’s superpowers has also raised questions about whether the gesture of sending giant pandas still works. China is massively different from how it used to be in the 1970s, and is currently embroiled in a wide range of issues, not only with the U.S., but also with other countries, which makes categorizing it neatly as a friend or foe less easy.
Ja Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, tells TIME that “the image of the pandas as soft, friendly, and cuddly—they don’t work today because a lot of [China’s aggressive] actions now are a lot more visible and fresh in people’s minds.”
“No one cares about pandas when national security or geostrategic interests come into play,” Tubilewicz added.
A 2022 peer-reviewed study at the University of Connecticut found that U.S. students who viewed panda videos that were not sourced from the government were likely to have a positive attitude toward Chinese culture and, in turn, Chinese people.
But while China’s practice of leasing pandas gives some people warm feelings, it makes others hot with anger. Conservationists and animal advocates have argued against using pandas as geopolitical pawns. Following the South Korea-China Summit earlier this year, the countries’ respective environmental officials discussed additional giant panda loans. But a Korean animal rights group slammed the move , saying that the creatures “are not beings born for human entertainment or interstate friendship.”
And many others are also starting to look past the panda diplomacy and demand other measures. A 2026 survey of U.S. adults conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago found that 28% of respondents said sending pandas to American zoos would improve their view of China, but much higher percentages said that more concrete actions like Chinese cooperation on curbing fentanyl precursors or easing trade restrictions would improve their view of China.
“The symbolism was still dominant in the 1970s,” Chong said. “It’s just that, given the lack of information, given the environment of that time, the symbolism probably got a lot more traction before than today.”
While surveys show many Americans are warming to China , Chong says “deep reservoirs of reservations remain,” particularly among Trump’s MAGA base: a July survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says that 63% of MAGA Republicans favor limiting the growth of Chinese power.
“Affection for pandas does not automatically translate into support for Chinese government policies,” Yu Tao, associate professor in Chinese Studies at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “Its more realistic contribution is to sustain public goodwill and opportunities for cooperation. The strongest case for panda diplomacy is that it gives people something they want to preserve in a relationship otherwise defined pretty much by disputes.”

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that the U.S. and China have reached agreements covering a subset of goods the two countries can trade on more favorable terms, marking fresh progress in negotiations between the world's two largest economies.
"We've actually reached agreement with the Chinese on a number of these things," Greer said on CNBC's "Squawk Box," referring to goods including U.S. agricultural products and medical devices and Chinese consumer goods considered non-sensitive.
Greer said the Trump administration plans to release "a lot more details" Monday about what the two sides have accomplished in negotiations over the past several weeks. He said the goal is to carve out areas of trade that could remain insulated from future tariff measures or broader trade disputes.
The two countries want some goods to be traded on a "more preferential basis" and potentially left aside if either country imposes new tariffs.
Greer did not specify Friday which products are covered by the agreements, how tariffs on those goods could change or when the new terms would take effect. Negotiations under the new U.S.-China "Board of Trade" mechanism are focused on "pure trade issues," Greer said, rather than U.S. national security restrictions on advanced technology.
"All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table," Greer said.
Trump and Xi, after they met in Beijing in May, announced the establishment of the "Board of Trade" to manage trade between the two rivals in non-sensitive products. Businesses have been waiting for more details on what categories of trade would be set aside, under the new framework, for lower tariffs.

Taylor Swift appeared to issue an apology to an ex-boyfriend in her new single Pink Clouding as she sang: 'I left scars on a good person - you didn't deserve it.'
The billionaire popstar, 36, dropped four new songs Patient Zero, Cleveland! Pink Clouding and Babylon on Friday, as an extended edition of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl.
And in The Encore's third new track Pink Clouding, it appears to not be about Taylor's husband Travis Kelce but instead sounds like it's about an ex-boyfriend who she didn't want to let down so ended things.
'Pink clouding', sometimes called Pink Cloud Syndrome, describes a period of intense optimism or euphoria that can occur early in addiction recovery before the realities and difficulties of recovery set back in.
The expression can also be used more broadly to describe a temporary euphoric state or the feeling that everything is suddenly rosy.
In the chorus, she sings: 'Cause I was pink clouding from the thrill of it (Pink) / Skydiving as you wrapped your arms around my body / Gray rocking where the arrow hit (Gray) / Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry / I didn't want to let you down (Pink cloud, pink cloud) / So I left you up there on a pink cloud (Pink, pink cloud).'

Fans speculated that Taylor was singing about ex Tom Hiddleston, who she dated in 2016 (pictured), as she sang that she didn't want to let him down so ended things
Taylor seems to apologize to this ex on the bridge, she sings: 'I hope / You realized my kind of trouble wasn't worth it / And the way I treated you, you never deserved it / And I swear to God, to this day / I wake up scared that I left scars on a good person / And I gave you zero reason to believe it / So be it / But it didn't mean nothing /Just 'cause I could leave it'
At the end of the song Taylor, who is famed for documenting her romantic woes through her music, says she hopes this guy 'landed safely on the ground' and 'I hope you're so happy now.'
It is unknown which of Taylor's exes the song is about but many fans speculated online that it could be about Tom Hiddleston who she dated in 2016.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Indexes Tick Higher at Open as Treasury Yields, Oil Prices Pull Back; Nasdaq, S&P 500 on Pace for Weekly Gains
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Indexes Tick Higher at Open as Treasury Yields, Oil Prices Pull Back; Nasdaq, S&P 500 on Pace for Weekly Gains
articles.content_orig:
The bond market is yelling at the Federal Reserve, but the messages are coming from different directions and pose a dilemma for policymakers as they seek to strike a balance that won't tank the economy.
Treasury yields continued their upward march Thursday as investors sought to price in a variety of factors: inflation still hovering well above the Fed's 2% goal, another bump up in energy prices and the impact of a global hyperscaler financial arms race and accompanying debt issuance.
In the past, policymakers have been willing to look through inflation spurts from temporary shocks like high energy prices and tariffs. And the narrative not so long ago was that the artificial intelligence investing boom was a story that would last a year or two and ultimately prove disinflationary.
But now Fed officials are rethinking the impact of those factors and seeing the danger of more durable inflation.
At the same time, markets are grappling with a central bank that suddenly has no interest in telegraphing its next moves, leaving an uncertain calculus on who is calling the shots — policymakers or market players.
"The time of looking through the initial supply shock has come to an end," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "The bias has to be towards restoring price stability, and they should take what's going on seriously."
Markets expect the central bank will indeed take a firmer hand on inflation.
Over the past day or so, traders raised the odds of a rate hike in October, which would come only a month or so after last week's quarter percentage point increase . They also see a third increase either late this year or early in 2027, with additional hikes possible in subsequent months.
That's a big switch from a Fed that in June projected it might hike once this year and then be done before starting to cut in the next couple of years.
"My view coming out of the [September] meeting was that we're going to get three rate hikes," Brusuelas said. But modeling performed at his firm about the potential for higher yields, along with a prolonged cycle of AI investment, changed that view.
The modeling indicated that sharply higher long-term yields could slow growth and increase unemployment and still not get inflation back to 2%. RSM found that even a 5.5% 10-year yield — it was around 5.15% on Thursday — would lower growth to 1.5% and lift unemployment to 4.7% while core inflation remained stuck at 2.4%.
"The Fed is underestimating what's going to be necessary to restore price stability — that we're probably not talking two or three hikes. We're talking five or six," Brusuelas said.
Not everyone on Wall Street agrees. Some strategists think the market is getting ahead of itself — that yields now essentially are pricing in stronger economic growth and are overly sensitive to the vagaries of oil prices amid the ongoing tensions in the Middle East.
"The rise in yields has not been due to expectations of a too-dovish Fed allowing inflation to persistently exceed target. Instead, the rise has been in real yields as investors priced-in the Fed setting higher policy rates," Citigroup economist Andrew Hollenhorst said in a note. "It should not be surprising that this has led to both higher shorter-term and longer-term yields."
Indeed, several key Fed officials, while endorsing near-term rate hikes, also are counseling patience.
New York Fed President John Williams , whose position puts him in the vice chair slot of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, said Thursday that it's "reasonable" to expect another hike by the end of the year, but also noted that officials need to keep watching the data before getting on a pre-set "forward guidance" track of locking in rate hikes.
Similarly, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson also indicated additional policy tightening is likely but characterized the potential moves as "modest," hardly an indication that she thinks a string of hikes is likely.
Still, the Fed faces a policy crossroads: Tighten too much and risk cutting off the expansion, or tighten too little and risk losing the market's faith that it is sufficiently tuned into inflation risks.
"Weak guidance guardrails risk putting ... central banks in a position where they may have to decide between a sub-optimal hike and disappointing the market and risking hard-won credibility," Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI, said in a note. "Lack of guidance also means whatever decision they take risks generating an outsized market response — either substantially further tightening or easing market rates."
Guha is in the camp that the market's expectations are "too aggressive" while also seeing the Fed's dilemma.
"Delivering back-to-back hikes — particularly without forward guidance as to how to interpret them — would risk sending a very hawkish signal that would reprice the rates curve further and to an unpredictable extent," Guha said. "But, skipping a hike priced odds-on in the market could also lead to a large repricing in the other dovish direction."
The conflict is critical now because Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has emphasized letting markets help guide policy. That's a big reversal from central bank policy since the global financial crisis in 2008, when the Fed used its forward-guidance tool to signal to investors which way rates were headed.
"His framework appears significantly less rooted in economic measurement details and significantly more reflective of market narratives," UBS economist Jonathan Pingle wrote of Warsh. "No Chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve has emphasized considering the signals from financial markets as an input into monetary policy decisions as strongly as Chairman Warsh."
With a yield surge that has taken the 30-year bond to its highest level since 2004, market dynamics have swung Warsh from someone calling for cuts prior to taking the job in May, to a chair who seems to have forged a hawkish coalition on the FOMC.
In fact, Pingle speculated that Warsh, following last week's post-meeting news conference, "left little doubt to us that his views more closely align" with Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, arguably one of the most hawkish of this year's voting group, "than anyone else on the FOMC."
For now, at least, markets are going with the interpretation that Warsh will let the Treasury market guide him toward progressively higher benchmark rates.
"There's a good reason why central bankers are beginning to be concerned about overheating in the investment section of the economy," said Brusuelas, the RSM economist. "Mr. Market is signaling something to policymakers like Kevin Warsh that they ought to listen to."
